items.title: 71542_Bill Coleman autobiographical manuscript
items.q: I didn't even hear of Kenny Dorham until he came over to France in 1949 for the Jazz Festival.

ctx.x: Things did not seem to have changed too much musically since I'd left. As far as trumpet players were concerned, even Dizzy Gillespie had not changed too much. He was still coming up. He had not, as yet, acquired a reputation. He got his name 'Dizzy' because he was a little wild, but apart from that people didn't consider him as any more than just another trumpet player. He didn't really start to emerge until after

he had left Cab Calloway. I appreciated the playing of Shad Collins and Roy Eldridge, but I didn't even hear of Kenny Dorham until he came over to France in 1949 for the Jazz Festival. I think at that time, Roy was still the 'king'.

The fourth of April, I recorded with Joe Marsala and his Delta Four, a session that was supervised by Leonard Feather. I had met Leonard in Paris where he came a few times to listen to certain jazz musicians as he was a critic of jazz music and wrote for the English musical paper 'Melody Maker'. Leonard had gone to New York at the beginning or shortly after the war started in 1939 and was later to become one of the editors of 'Down Beat', which was the best jazz magazine in the States at one time.
